title: Manna Festival Finals Tax
subject: Constitutional Law
stem:
After several costly nationwide flood-control projects, Congress enacted the Manna Festival Finals Revenue Act as part of a broader plan to retire federal disaster-recovery debt. For six years, the Act imposed a 40% excise tax on the price of paid admission wristbands to final-round artisan food competitions. Covered events included the Manna Bread Cup, the Loaves-and-Fishes Fish-Fry Crown, the Ruth Harvest Pie Finals, and similar paid championship food contests.

This federal tax is probably

choices.A: unconstitutional, because Congress violates the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment by taxing final-round artisan food competitions while failing to tax other large paid food festivals.
choices.B: unconstitutional, because a 40% admission tax is likely to reduce attendance at these final-round competitions and, therefore, is not rationally related to Congress’s legitimate interest in retiring disaster-recovery debt.
choices.C: constitutional, because an act of Congress that appears to be a revenue-raising measure on its face is not rendered invalid because it may have adverse economic consequences for the activity taxed.
choices.D: constitutional, because the compelling national interest in retiring federal disaster-recovery debt justifies this tax as a temporary emergency measure.

rightExplanation: C is correct. The Act is framed as a revenue measure: it imposes an excise tax on paid admissions and is tied to retiring federal debt. Gold Key: A federal tax that is facially revenue-raising is not invalid merely because it burdens, discourages, or economically harms the taxed activity. Silver Key: In this array, first lock the call as a federal taxing-power question; then distrust the answers that import strict scrutiny, equal protection, or attendance-impact framing without a trigger.

c3.label: CUT A
c3.text: The answer invents an all-or-nothing tax rule: if Congress taxes this event category, it must tax neighboring paid events. That rule is not in the stem. Gold Key confirms the tax-classification deference.

c3.label: CUT B
c3.text: The answer’s reason does not carry its conclusion. Reduced attendance does not prove the tax lacks a revenue relationship.

c3.label: CUT D
c3.text: The answer imports strict-scrutiny language. The stem gives no suspect class, fundamental right, or protected constitutional trigger.

c3.label: Residual
c3.text: C remains. No CLASH or CALL is needed after the anchor-assisted cuts.

studentScript: Tax frame. No protected trigger. Cut strict scrutiny. Cut attendance non sequitur. Cut all-or-nothing equal protection. Pick the revenue-tax answer.

A.signal: The answer claims Congress violates equal protection just by taxing one event category and not similar categories.
A.lawyer: Economic and tax classifications receive rational-basis deference absent a suspect class or fundamental-right trigger.

B.signal: The reason does not support the conclusion: lower attendance does not erase the revenue relationship.
B.lawyer: A tax is not invalid merely because it burdens or discourages the taxed activity.

C.signal: This answer matches the call and stays in the tax/revenue frame.
C.lawyer: Congress has Article I taxing power; a facial revenue tax is not invalid merely because of adverse economic consequences.

D.signal: The answer imports compelling-interest language without a trigger.
D.lawyer: Tax measures of this kind do not need strict scrutiny absent a separate protected-right or suspect-class trigger.

goldKeys.statement: A federal excise tax that is facially revenue-raising is usually valid even if it burdens, discourages, or economically harms the taxed activity.
goldKeys.trigger: federal excise tax + revenue/debt purpose + argument that the tax hurts the taxed activity
goldKeys.authority: U.S. Const. art. I, §8; Sonzinsky v. United States; Fernandez v. Wiener

goldKeys.statement: Ordinary economic and tax classifications do not get strict scrutiny unless the stem gives a suspect class, fundamental right, or other protected trigger.
goldKeys.trigger: tax classification + compelling-interest or equal-protection answer with no protected trigger
goldKeys.authority: Regan v. Taxation With Representation; FCC v. Beach Communications

silverKeys.statement: When a Con Law tax array mixes compelling interest, rational relation, equal protection, and economic-impact language, first lock the question as taxing power before liking the strongest-sounding constitutional phrase.
silverKeys.trigger: revenue tax stem with multiple constitutional standards in the answer set
silverKeys.unlocks: taxing-power frame vs imported scrutiny frames

remediation.title: Tax-power frame before scrutiny frame
remediation.signal: Federal excise tax + revenue purpose + answer choices invoking strict scrutiny or equal protection.
remediation.studentMove: Ask whether the stem gives a protected trigger. If not, stay in the revenue-tax frame.
remediation.tinyRule: Bad economic effects do not by themselves invalidate a facial revenue tax.
remediation.trap: Picking the dramatic constitutional standard instead of the tax-power answer.
